Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPA This Is India World news As conflict in the Middle East intensifies, India’s relationship with Israel deepens An Amnesty International report reveals that the country is now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. Plus, Assam floods, student anger spreads and a song to put in rotation Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Niha Masih Tue 11 Aug 2026 02.55 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 04.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hello, and welcome back to This Is India . For this week’s newsletter, I’m looking at India’s evolving relationship with Israel, and how it has deepened as conflict swept across the Middle East. Why is it that India has formed an even closer bond with a country that has faced mounting international isolation and backlash over a military campaign in Gaza that has left the territory in ruins and killed more than 70,000 Palestinians , – many of whom were children? Under Narendra Modi, India’s ties with Israel have taken on a different character, for a country that once championed the Palestinian cause and led the Non-Aligned Movement. To better understand it, I turned to Stanly Johny, Indian foreign policy expert and the international affairs editor at the Hindu. He told me it isn’t just a political or diplomatic shift, “it’s also at the strategic and defence level”. The evolution of India’s role was revealed in a recent Amnesty International investigation, which showed that India was now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. This represents a fundamental change. For years, New Delhi had primarily been a major customer of Israeli weapons. But, through joint ventures and manufacturing partnerships, it is now a “significant contributor” to Israel’s weapons production, according to Amnesty , which offers the most extensive account so far of the scale of India’s involvement since the war in Gaza began. Indian companies, including state-owned enterprises, have delivered drone warheads, artillery shell casings, small arms parts and military vehicle components to Israeli military suppliers despite the substantial risk these could end up in weapons deployed in Gaza, it added. By examining publicly available shipment-level trade data, Amnesty said it traced hundreds of thousands of weapons components shipped from Indian factories to Israeli military suppliers between 7 October 2023 and 30 November 2025, including: 390,516 small arms parts for military grade weapons 564,970 parts of explosive ordnance 298 components of military vehicles Many western nations, including Britain, have restricted or banned arms supply to Israel over its conduct in the war, citing risks that the weapons could be used to commit or facilitate violations of international humanitarian law. (The United States accounts for the overwhelming share of major arms transfers to Israel.) An independent United Nations commission of inquiry concluded in September that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza , and earlier this year another commission found that Israel is continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children . Separately, the international criminal court has issued an arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of committing war crimes. Yet, the Amnesty report hasn’t resulted in any large-scale public debate or political backlash in India, despite some scattered media coverage. Johny believes this is a result of the support for Israel by Modi’s voter base. “There is a clear ideological confluence between Hindutva and Zionism,” he said. In rightwing circles in India and elsewhere, he argues, Israel is increasingly seen as a bulwark against the expansion of Islam. View image in fullscreen Modi has long cultivated a personal rapport with Netanyahu. Photograph: Kobi Gideon Hindu nationalists have long admired Israel, viewing it as a model of a nationalist state that can assert itself in a volatile neighbourhood. Author Pankaj Mishra chronicled this affinity in a 2017 essay , writing that his grandfather was among high-caste Hindus who saw Israel as an example of how to deal with Muslims “in the only language they understood: that of force and more force”. The war on Gaza doesn’t appear to have significantly shifted views. A Pew Research survey published in June found that more Indians view Israel favourably (32%) than unfavourably (28%). This is in contrast to the decline of support for Israel in many western countries, including the United States, since the war. Modi, for his part, has cultivated a personal rapport with Netanyahu. In 2017, he became the first Indian prime minister to visit Israel , and Modi’s visit to Israel earlier this year came just 48 hours before Israel and the United States launched their attacks on Iran. The optics of Modi hugging Netanyahu on the tarmac, coupled with New Delhi’s noticeably muted response at the outbreak of war, were a clear sign of where India’s political establishment stands. It has not gone unnoticed. In July, after the US vice-president, JD Vance, rebuked Netanyahu by calling the US Israel’s “only powerful ally” left in the world, Netanyahu shot back : “We have some other friends, like a small country called India. It has 1.4bn people, and boy, do we have tremendous support there.” The government has previously declined to give a direct answer about weapons supplies to Israel. When asked in parliament in 2024 , external affairs minister S Jaishankar said that information is not in public domain and that exports of military products are guided by “national interest”. Amnesty identified three state-owned Indian companies – Munitions India Limited, India Optel Limited and Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited – supplying Israel with weapons, which it said, could expose India to the hazard of “complicity in ongoing genocide in Gaza”. Foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal responded that India’s exports are governed by national laws and international obligations. The pushback has largely come from human rights activists, student bodies, trade unions, India’s left-leaning parties and the Congress party . The courts have offered no recourse, either. In 2024, a group of civil servants, activists and academics petitioned the supreme court , demanding India suspend its military exports to Israel. The court dismissed the case, ruling that the matter fell within the discretion of the executive. “In India, you don’t see any anger towards the government for its relationship with Israel, despite the allegations the Israeli government is facing,” Johny said. This, he believes, is a sign that foreign policy debates in India are being stripped of moral concern. Weapons aren’t the only thing India has sent to Israel during this period. Thousands of Indian workers have also gone to Israel, in many instances to replace Palestinians barred from entering the country after 7 October 2023. Last year, the government told parliament that more than 20,000 Indian workers , in construction work and caregiving, had moved to Israel after an agreement signed in November 2023. India, meanwhile, has shored up its own arms supplies from Israel. Between 2021 and 2025, New Delhi was Israel’s largest defence customer, accounting for 29% of total arms sales, according to Stockholm International Peace Research Institute . But for Johny, India’s growing closeness to Israel is beginning to come at a cost. The war in Iran threatens India’s energy security and could have wider economic repercussions across the Gulf, home to a large Indian diaspora. “India has to continue to stay engaged with Israel, but it is important to restore balance to its approach to west Asia,” he said, adding that it needs to forcefully defend its own interests. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c141.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Firefighters work at the site of a book market hit by a Russian missile strike in Kyiv By Dan Johnson ,Â Ukraine correspondent, in Kyiv, Â and Â Tinshui Yeung Published 16 August 2026, 09:14 BST Updated 1 hour ago At least five people have been killed and more than 10 injured in Ukraine in the latest wave of Russian strikes, officials have said. The attacks caused fires across the capital, Kyiv, including at a book market, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said, accusing Russia of targeting civilian infrastructure. Meanwhile, Moscow's mayor said about 600 Ukrainian drones were launched towards the city overnight. A warehouse belonging to Russian online retailer Wildberries was hit. Seven people have died across Russia, officials said. Russia has intensified aerial attacks across Ukraine in recent weeks, while Kyiv has stepped up attacks on Russian logistics hubs, aiming to disrupt military supplies. Air-raid sirens have sounded four times since Saturday night in Kyiv. At least six people, including a child, were reportedly injured, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. The mayor of Kryvyi Rih said a 44-year-old man earlier reported missing had been found dead in rubble. Another person was killed and 14 workers of a steel plant were wounded there. Two people in their 60s were killed when a house was destroyed in Zaporizhzhia, while a person was also killed in Sumy, according to the Ukrainian president. Figure caption, Watch: Footage shows huge plumes of smoke rising into the sky Zelensky said the cities of Kremenchuk and Kryvyi Rih were hit by ballistic missiles, adding: "Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure." Russia said its attacks on Kyiv on Saturday night targeted a FirePoint facility producing parts for Ukrainian Flamingo missiles and a factory making components for drones. A book market in the city's Pochayna district was damaged in the strikes. Burnt books could be seen lying on the ground, while firefighters continue to douse the flames. Sixty-nine-year-old Valentina's husband owned a market stall. Looking through the rubble, she told the BBC: "All these books in the street were from my husband's stall in the market - I recognise them on the floor." She added: "You never think that it will happen to you." Image caption, Valentina said these books belonged to her husband's business Vinyl store owner Luba, 42, said she has lost 500,000 hryvnias (Â£8,262) worth of stock. "This business was my baby - many of the vinyls destroyed were rare and irreplaceable," she told the BBC. "I want Russia to disappear from this Earth." The country's defence ministry also said it hit the Kremenchuk oil refinery in Poltava region, which it said supplied fuel to the Ukrainian military. Moscow said it struck a steelworks in Kryvyi Rih it said had been making weapons components. Russia also said it hit a dry cargo vessel near Odesa, claiming it had been carrying military equipment. Zelensky said 13 regions had come under attack this week, with Russia launching more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided aerial bombs and 62 missiles. In Russia, air defences intercepted and destroyed 822 Ukrainian drones, according to its defence ministry. Figure caption, Watch: The BBC's Dan Johnson says fighting between Ukraine and Russia has intensified The governor of Rostov in south-western Russia said five people died following overnight strikes, while his counterpart in the Belgorod region bordering Ukraine said a woman was killed after a bus was struck. A drone attack on Moscow killed an 83-year-old man after it crashed. Three people were also injured in an overnight Ukrainian strike in Moscow, its Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said. He added that roughly a third of the drones Ukraine launched at the capital had been destroyed. A Wildberries warehouse in Koledino, 25km (15.5 miles) from the centre of Moscow, was hit in the attack, Sobyanin said. Videos shows a fire and a large plume of smoke over the warehouse. Wildberries, known as Russia's version of Amazon, has been repeatedly targeted since July. Kyiv said at the time it was targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment and disrupting supplies to the Russian army. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Wildberries has been the target of multiple Ukrainian attacks Meanwhile, the Romanian defence ministry said a Spanish fighter jet shot down a drone that had breached its airspace near the border with Ukraine and Moldova. The drone entered from Moldova and was intercepted by an F-18 deployed on Nato duties at 05:01 local time (02:01 GMT) on Sunday, the ministry said in a statement. Debris fell in an unpopulated area of the Galati region, near the Ukrainian border, it added. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory. With marginal gains being made by either side in an attritional ground battle along a lengthy front line, the war has predominantly become an aerial one, with exchanges of missiles and drones aimed at degrading each country's warfighting ability. Image: Dmitry Feoktistov/TASS/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement The independent Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced that it is shutting down and ceasing operations under pressure from state authorities who recently searched the home of its senior editor. "They've killed us," read a statement published on the newspaper's website on Friday morning. "The Russian authorities — the Russian special services — have forced the editorial team to end its work," added editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov in a video statement. "On November 9 we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave." What is the Novaya Gazeta ? Founded in 1993 following the collapse of the Soviet Union , the Novaya Gazeta (Russian for "New Newspaper") was one of the few remaining critical media outlets in Russia , known for its investigations into corruption and its critical coverage of Russian politics. It has always operated under pressure from state authorities but circumstances have deteriorated dramatically since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, with the Kremlin introducing near-Soviet levels of media censorship . The vast majority of independent journalists have been forced into exile and those who have remained in Russia have been designated "foreign agents" — a label which imposes a wide range of restrictions in everyday life including on the right to earn income from rent, interest payments or royalties from intellectual work. A former Novaya Gazeta editor-in-chief, ​ Dmitry Muratov , dedicated his 2021 Nobel Peace ​Prize to six colleagues who were killed because ​of their work — including Anna Politkovskaya , who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by the Russian military in Chechnya and was found dead in her apartment block on President Vladimir Putin 's birthday in October 2006. "More than 30 years of life together with our country and its citizens will now end on the street," wrote the newspaper in its editorial, "without a basis for existence and under constant threat of repression." The announcement of the outlet's closure comes two weeks after veteran editor-in-chief Sokolov was questioned by investigators in Moscow over "unlawful use of personal data" in connection with a criminal case against a colleague, Oleg Roldugin. Roldugin had been detained and charged with obtaining "unlawful access to computerized information," an offence that carries a prison term of up to 10 years. No further details were given and Roldugin has pleaded not guilty. International media rights groups have slammed the targeting of the Novaya Gazeta , with Reporters Without Borders calling on the Kremlin to "put an end to the judicial harassment" of its journalists. Novaya Gazeta : 'The story of a country and a society being finished off' In its editorial, the Novaya Gazeta wrote that its closure reflected the state of modern Russia under President Putin. "This isn't just our personal story; it's the story of a country and a society that are being finished off in exactly the same way," it wrote. "Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated and their protection has been equated with a crime. Elections and elected bodies have been de facto eliminated. Public institutions have been dismantled. Freedom of conscience and human dignity have been trampled. Private life has been turned inside out by dirty hands. "The courts have been destroyed, along with the law and the rule of law. Holding one's own convictions is now treason. But treason is when a state betrays its own Constitution. And this treason is an ongoing crime, currently unfolding before the eyes of the entire world." Oleshky ceasefire comes into effect in Ukraine war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Oleshky: evacuations begin amid localized truce Meanwhile, in Ukraine , the evacuation of stranded residents from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky began on Friday as a localized US-brokered ceasefire continued to hold into a fourth day. Captured by Russian troops early in the war in 2022, locals had endured food, water and medicine shortages for months, with some being forced to hunt and eat pigeons, residents told the AFP news agency. The population of Oleshky has since dropped from 24,000 to about 2,000, many of whom were on Friday set to be evacuated either to Russian-controlled or Ukrainian-controlled territory. "Evacuation and distribution of humanitarian aid have begun," said Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia while Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova posted a video showing groups of people waiting to board buses. The local ceasefire — announced by US First Lady Melania Trump last week — is the longest pause in fighting anywhere in Ukraine since the 2022 invasion. It is due to end on Sunday evening.
